newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka navy to probe $63 million ammunition deal.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka navy to probe $63 million ammunition deal.

text.p: The Sri Lankan navy is investigating a $63 million arms deal that will leave the country with a 30-year stockpile of ammunition when its actual shelf-life is only five years.
"There is an investigation going on. Unfortunately we can't give any more details at this point," a senior navy official, who asked to remain unidentified, told Reuters.
The independent Island newspaper said on Sunday that $63 million worth of Chinese-made ammunition had been sitting in Colombo port since mid-January.
It said Navy chief Admiral Cecil Tissera, who took over several months after the Chinese-made ammunition was believed to have been ordered, had appointed a naval official to conduct a probe.

The ammunition included 300 tonnes of 37 millimetre and 200 tonnes of 25 millimetre high-explosive shells, to be used on the navy's ageing Chinese-built gunboats which have been in service since 1972, the Island newspaper said.

Six Shanghai-class gunboats spearhead the navy's fleet in its battle against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, who are waging war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east.
The newspaper quoted defence sources who said even at the current rate of usage, it would take the navy some 30 years to use up the stockpile of shells.

"This means that unless the armed forces are trying to start a war with another country, around 80 percent of this ammunition will have to be disposed in approximately five years time," the newspaper said.
It also said the navy had plans to phase out its 37 mm and 25 mm guns by the end of this year.

The Sri Lankan government has allocated 44 billion rupees ($754 million) for defence this year, of which the navy gets about 6.7 billion rupees. Defence spending in calendar 1997 will account for about 22 percent of total government spending.
The navy chief told Reuters earlier this month the navy needed to triple its fleet of 100-plus craft of various types to meet the threat from the Tamil Tigers' formidable "Sea Tiger" naval wing.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war, now in its 14th year. The Tigers say the toll is higher. (1$ = 58.68)
